title: What I've been reading - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Cowen's reading roundup covers Mike Jay on brain technology, Grossman's WWII front-line dispatches, the Iranian poet Forough Farrokhzad, Breton's Nadja, and Emma Southon on Roman slavery — with a recurring stance that most canonical past works are not masterpieces and that partial reading is often optimal.

insights.claim: Cowen explicitly endorses not finishing books, recommending Grossman's Stalingrad-Treblinka-Berlin dispatches on the basis that only the best third justifies the time because the rest repeats.
insights.so_what: A reusable information-diet rule: optimize for the highest-signal fraction of a source rather than completion, which applies directly to research reports and filings.
insights.quote: You do not have to read the whole thing, as there is some degree of repetition.
insights.locator: 2. Vasily Grossman, From the Front Line
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Cowen's positive test for a nonfiction book is density plus generativity — whether it is substantive on every page and whether it pushes you toward its own cited sources.
insights.so_what: A crisp quality screen for research: does it hold information per page, and does it expand your source graph?
insights.quote: An excellent book, substantive on every page, and it will make you want to read some of the works he cites.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Cowen argues most surviving works from the past are not masterpieces, using Breton's Nadja as the case that literary reputation can persist long after the work stops delivering.
insights.so_what: Canonical status is a poor proxy for present value — survivorship in reputation markets is sticky and mispriced.
insights.quote: But one learns most books from the past are not masterpieces
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Within surrealism, the painting output mattered far more than the literary output, so the movement's historical importance is concentrated in one medium rather than spread evenly.
insights.so_what: Within a 'movement' or a theme, value is usually concentrated in one channel; buying the theme broadly dilutes the actual driver.
insights.quote: surrealism as a movement — most of all in painting — was more important than the literary outputs of surrealism
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Cowen breaks his own rule against translated poetry for Forough Farrokhzad, who died at 33 in a 1967 car crash, while flagging that the Farsi original is probably both better and materially different.
insights.so_what: When a source is strong enough to break a stated prior, that is the highest-information kind of recommendation.
insights.quote: I usually do not enjoy poetry in translation, but this is so fiery and full of passion that I am happy to recommend it.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen

insights.claim: Cowen sides with Emma Southon's harsher reading of Roman slavery over rival interpretations, while conceding that disputes about antiquity are generally not resolvable on evidence.
insights.so_what: Note the epistemic move: adopting a position on intuition while flagging that the underlying evidence cannot settle it — a useful disclosure standard.
insights.quote: While my general view is that interpretative disputes over antiquity are difficult to resolve, I find her interpretations more intuitive and more convincing than the other side of the debate.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
